clue.text: Weapon for creator of Utopia on earth

blocks.note: clay is a kind of earth
Sir Thomas More wrote Utopia

explanation.surface: Someone asks what weapon the author of Utopia carried here on earth.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas More's Utopia (1516) describes an imaginary ideal island; 'on' places his name after the earth word.
explanation.definitionFit: A claymore is a large two-handed Scottish sword, so it is a kind of weapon.

clue.text: Room in bank hard to get inside

indicators.note: a thing that gets inside another is placed within it

blocks.note: a camber is the slope or banking of a road surface
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A bank vault room that is difficult to break into.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamber is a room, especially a private or official one.

clue.text: Judgment of a friend includes endless approval)

indicators.note: one thing including another holds it within
without an end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
praise is expressed approval

explanation.surface: A friend's verdict contains unending praise.
explanation.definitionFit: An appraisal is an assessment or evaluation, a considered judgment of worth.

clue.text: Power to capture both rooks giving brilliant mate

indicators.note: capturing pieces means taking them in, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: might is power or strength
R is the chess notation for rook, twice

explanation.surface: A chess move takes both of the opponent's rooks and leads to a fine checkmate.
explanation.walkthrough: The chess setting makes mate look like checkmate; it is a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Right is the ideal husband or partner someone hopes to find, a perfect mate.

clue.text: Joiner knocked up last of three piece suite

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from the bottom, so it runs backwards
the last of a word is its final letter only

blocks.note: something that unites things is a joiner
the final letter of the word three

explanation.surface: A carpenter has hastily built the final element of a three-piece suite of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-piece suite is a sofa and two armchairs; here suite means the attendants of an important person.
explanation.definitionFit: A suite can be a group of attendants accompanying a dignitary, which is a retinue.

clue.text: Motorway madness is an illusion

blocks.note: the M1, Britain's first motorway, written as if with the letter I
rage is a fit of madness or fury

explanation.surface: Road rage on a motorway is dismissed as a delusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London-to-Leeds motorway; crosswords read its name as the letters MI.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, such as shimmering water seen on a hot road.

clue.text: Such a painting calls for quite a little skill

definitions.text: Such a painting calls for quite a little skill

blocks.clueFragment: Such a painting calls for quite a little skill
blocks.note: surface reading: this sort of picture needs only modest talent
setter's reading: the painting is very small, and small-scale work needs fine skill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite a little skill' sounds like 'not much talent', but it means a lot of skill for something tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A miniature is a very small, finely detailed painting, often a portrait, and the word also means tiny.

clue.text: Taking exercise like a gentleman?

blocks.note: surface reading: jogging, the commonest way to take exercise
setter's reading: the question mark hints at a second sense of the same word, as a candidate for office is said to be doing

explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both jogging and standing for office; the question mark warns that the gentleman is not simply out for exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Going at a jog is the usual meaning, and a candidate seeking election is also described with this word.

clue.text: He complains poor organiser is missing

indicators.note: the two letters spelling the word is go missing from the longer word
a poor version is a badly made one, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written before letters are lost

explanation.surface: A grumbler moans that the event organiser has not turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: A groaner is a person who moans or grumbles, someone who complains.

clue.text: Eliza's aim?

blocks.note: surface reading: what Eliza is striving towards, her ambition
setter's reading: Eliza Doolittle of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady drops her aitches, so her lessons aim at sounding the letter H

explanation.walkthrough: Eliza Doolittle must learn to pronounce her Hs; sounding an H is the technical sense of the answer, which also means an ambition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a hope or ambition and the breathy H sound in speech, which Eliza had to learn.

clue.text: Time to return, all the same

indicators.note: if a word looks all the same when it comes back the other way, it reads identically in both directions

blocks.note: midday, a time of day, which reads identically either way

explanation.surface: It is time to go back, everything being equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Noon is twelve o'clock midday, a particular time of day.

clue.text: Something synthesizer's capable of for 50s group

blocks.note: first meaning: a synthesizer can produce rhythms, a drum track
second meaning: the literary movement of Kerouac and Ginsberg in the 1950s

explanation.surface: An electronic keyboard is praised as just right for a fifties band.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, a synthesizer is capable of generating a beat; the same phrase names the 1950s American writers Kerouac, Ginsberg and Burroughs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the literal act of producing rhythm and the name of the 1950s American literary movement.

clue.text: Repeated performance to capture some tennis prize

indicators.note: capturing something means holding it inside, so one word takes the other within it

blocks.note: rote is mechanical repetition, as in learning by rote
a set is a portion of a tennis match

explanation.surface: An encore performance wins a tennis trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosette is a ribbon badge awarded as a prize at shows and competitions.

clue.text: Composed a rebuttal that settled old scores?

indicators.note: something composed is put together, so these letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: every letter used

explanation.surface: A written counter-argument that put an end to long-running grudges.
explanation.walkthrough: Settling old scores suggests revenge; here old scores are musical scores written down.
explanation.definitionFit: Tablature was the old system of musical notation for lute and similar instruments, a way of fixing scores on paper.

clue.text: Cutting consultation with MP

blocks.note: first meaning: operating with a knife in a hospital
second meaning: a session where constituents meet their Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A sharp, cutting meeting with a Member of Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: British MPs hold regular sessions, called by the same name as a doctor's consulting hours, where constituents bring problems.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both operative medical treatment and an MP's or doctor's advice session for the public.

clue.text: Get rid of queen and ace, then require to discard heart

indicators.note: throwing away the heart of a word removes its central letter

blocks.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
to dictate is to lay down what is required

explanation.surface: A card game: dispose of the queen and ace, then you must throw away a heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The cards make heart look like the suit; it means the middle letter of a seven-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: To eradicate is to destroy completely or root out, so it means to get rid of.

clue.text: Silly man holding a black jumper

indicators.note: one thing holding others keeps them inside it

blocks.note: a wally is British slang for a foolish man
taken as written
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A foolish fellow is clutching a black sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper in Britain is a sweater, which is the surface sense; here it is an animal that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallaby is a small kangaroo-like marsupial that moves by hopping, so it is a jumper.

clue.text: Ran off furiously, beginning to take offence

indicators.note: acting furiously means wildly, so these letters are thrown into disorder
the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: these six letters rearranged
the opening letter of take

explanation.surface: Someone stormed off angrily, starting to feel insulted.
explanation.definitionFit: An affront is an insult, a deliberate slight that causes offence.

clue.text: Bay I heard was dangerous to sail near

indicators.note: what is heard is judged by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: bay is the laurel tree, followed by I

explanation.surface: Someone recalls hearing that a certain bay was hazardous to sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lorelei is a rock on the Rhine where, in legend, a siren lured boatmen to their deaths; the definition describes it in the past tense, as the clue does.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Rhine siren on her rock drew sailors to wreck, so she was perilous to approach.

clue.text: Regrets bird no longer existing in the mountains

indicators.note: a thing found in a place sits inside it, so one word goes within the other

blocks.note: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain peak, as in Ben Nevis
the moa was a giant flightless New Zealand bird, now extinct

explanation.surface: Someone laments an extinct bird that once lived in the highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: To bemoan is to express regret or sorrow about something, so bemoans can replace regrets.

clue.text: Trust is what's central to agent about to have double existence

indicators.note: what is central to a word is its middle letter
about means around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: two words meaning exist: be and live
the middle letter of the five-letter word agent

explanation.surface: A spy at the heart of a trust is about to lead a double life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double existence' suggests a double agent; it asks for two words for exist side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To believe someone is to trust them, accepting what they say as true.

clue.text: Doctor ready to film disappearance of satellite

blocks.note: MO is a medical officer
on set means in place for filming

explanation.surface: A doctor is all prepared to shoot a movie about a vanishing satellite.
explanation.walkthrough: Satellite suggests a spacecraft; here it is the Moon, Earth's natural satellite.
explanation.definitionFit: Moonset is the time the Moon sinks below the horizon, when Earth's satellite vanishes from sight.

clue.text: Propose going eventually to split up drunken guests

indicators.note: what comes eventually comes at the end, so only the last letter is kept
a piece that splits up a word goes into its middle
a drunken thing staggers about, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the final letter of going
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone suggests going home at last to break up the party of tipsy visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest something is to put it forward for consideration, which is what propose means.

clue.text: Progressive goal - find work or bust

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the preceding words fall apart and are rebuilt

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: An ambitious motto: get a job or go broke.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone progressive looks to the future and favours new ideas, which is what forward-looking describes.

clue.text: Consort with criminal in Flanders

blocks.note: first meaning: a gangster's girlfriend
second meaning: the first name of Defoe's heroine ... Flanders

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of associating with a lawbreaker in Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: Flanders looks like the region of Belgium; it is the surname of Daniel Defoe's novel's heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: A moll is a gangster's female companion, and Moll is also the given name of Defoe's Flanders heroine.

clue.text: Liable to bad taste? Don't exaggerate

indicators.note: something gone bad is spoiled, so the following word is spoiled into a new order

blocks.note: being under something, such as a duty, means being subject or liable to it
its five letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A query about poor taste, followed by advice not to overstate things.
explanation.definitionFit: To understate is to describe something as less than it is, the opposite of exaggerating; the imperative fits.

clue.text: Missed ball in one US sport - everything hit in another

definitions.text: Missed ball in one US sport

blocks.clueFragment: Missed ball in one US sport
blocks.note: first meaning: in baseball, a swing that fails to hit the pitch
second meaning: in ten-pin bowling, knocking down all the pins with the first ball

explanation.surface: A comparison of two American games, one about missing and one about hitting everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Strike names both a baseball miss and a bowling score where all ten pins fall at once.

clue.text: It's safe to go over shoulder on motorway

definitions.text: It's safe to go over shoulder on motorway

blocks.clueFragment: It's safe to go over shoulder on motorway
blocks.note: surface reading: it is safe to drive onto the hard shoulder of the motorway
setter's reading: the thing that goes across your shoulder in the car and keeps you safe

explanation.walkthrough: The hard shoulder is the emergency lane of a British motorway, so the clue seems to be driving advice; in fact a car's restraint strap runs over the occupant's shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's diagonal safety strap crosses the wearer's shoulder and keeps them secure while travelling.
